Networks are piecewise linear, so the same attack works on them with $w$ replaced by the input gradient: the **fast gradient sign method** takes
$$
\delta = \epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_x \ell(h_\theta(x), y)\big).
$$

**Adversarial training** (Madry et al. 2018) solves
$$
\min_\theta \mathbb{E}\max_{\|\delta\|_\infty \leq \epsilon}\ell(h_\theta(x + \delta), y),
$$
approximating the inner maximum by a few projected gradient steps — a minimax (saddle-point) problem, the subject of ch. 8 of the Optimization for AI notes (optional reading) — at a cost of several forward-backward passes per training step.
:::

::: note
[Distribution shift]{.tag} The second robustness question needs no adversary: deployment data differ from training data (another hospital, another camera, corruptions such as blur or noise). The honest protocol evaluates on held-out shifted sets, not only on an i.i.d. test split, and reports the drop. Data augmentation, pre-training on broad data and the equivariances of ch. 1 are the usual levers; none removes the drop entirely.
:::

### 7.2. Deep reinforcement learning {#dl-rl}

In reinforcement learning no label says what the right output is: an agent acts, the environment answers with a new state and a reward, and the goal is to maximize the accumulated reward. Deep networks enter as function approximators for values or policies over large state spaces (pixels, board positions, text).

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — Markov decision process, values, Bellman equation]{.tag} A Markov decision process has states $s$, actions $a$, transition probabilities $P(s' \mid s, a)$, rewards $r(s, a)$ and a discount $\gamma \in [0, 1)$.

A policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ generates trajectories $\tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \dots)$ with return $R(\tau) = \sum_{t \geq 0}\gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)$. The action value $Q^\pi(s, a)$ is the expected return when starting with $(s, a)$ and following $\pi$ afterwards. The optimal action value satisfies the **Bellman optimality equation**
$$
Q^\star(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P(\cdot \mid s, a)}\max_{a'}Q^\star(s', a'),
$$
and acting greedily with respect to $Q^\star$ is optimal.
:::

**Value-based deep RL.** Deep Q-networks (Mnih et al. 2015) fit a network $Q_\theta$ to the Bellman equation by minimizing
$$
\big(r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q_{\theta^-}(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a)\big)^2
$$
over transitions $(s, a, r, s')$.

Two devices make it stable: a **replay buffer** of past transitions, sampled at random to break the correlation of consecutive steps, and a **target network** $\theta^-$, a copy of $\theta$ refreshed only every few thousand steps, so that the regression target does not move at every update.

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.5 — Policy gradient (REINFORCE, Williams 1992)]{.tag} For a differentiable policy $\pi_\theta$ and $J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[R(\tau)]$ (finite horizon $T$),
$$
\nabla J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[R(\tau)\sum_{t=0}^{T}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\Big],
$$
and the identity still holds when $R(\tau)$ is replaced by $R(\tau) - b$ for any constant baseline $b$.

The gradient can thus be estimated from sampled trajectories, without knowing or differentiating the dynamics.

::: proof
This is [theorem 5.1 of the RL course](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch5) (mandatory, same period, session 7), proved there in full. In short: the initial distribution and the dynamics do not depend on $\theta$, so
$$
\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau) = \sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t),
$$
and the log-derivative trick $\nabla p_\theta = p_\theta\,\nabla\log p_\theta$ turns $\nabla J = \sum_\tau R(\tau)\nabla p_\theta(\tau)$ into the stated expectation. The baseline drops out because
$$
\mathbb{E}[\nabla\log p_\theta(\tau)] = \nabla\sum_\tau p_\theta(\tau) = \nabla 1 = 0 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 7.6 — Policy gradient on a two-armed bandit]{.tag} One state, two actions; action $1$ gives reward $1$, action $0$ gives $0$; the policy plays action $1$ with probability $\pi_\theta(1) = \sigma(\theta)$, the logistic function.

Then
$$
J(\theta) = \sigma(\theta) \quad\text{and}\quad J'(\theta) = \sigma(\theta)(1 - \sigma(\theta)).
$$

-   **Without baseline.** The REINFORCE estimator is $r\cdot\partial_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a)$: it equals $1 - \sigma(\theta)$ when action $1$ is drawn (probability $\sigma(\theta)$) and $0$ otherwise, so its mean is $\sigma(\theta)(1 - \sigma(\theta))$, as the theorem says.
-   **With the baseline $b = \tfrac12$**, the estimator becomes $\tfrac12(1 - \sigma(\theta))$ for action $1$ and $\tfrac12\sigma(\theta)$ for action $0$, since
    $$
    \partial_\theta\log(1 - \sigma(\theta)) = -\sigma(\theta) :
    $$
    same mean.

    At $\theta = 0$ it takes the constant value $\tfrac14$, whereas without baseline it takes the values $\tfrac12$ and $0$ — the baseline removed all the variance at that point.

Actor-critic methods and PPO, used to fine-tune language models from human feedback, learn such baselines with a value network. The [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) module of the same period treats the field in depth.
:::

::: note
[The cost of RLHF on a 7B model, in the units of this module]{.tag} Fine-tuning a language model from human feedback with PPO (Ouyang et al. 2022) keeps four networks of the same size in play: the policy and a value network, both trained (16 bytes per parameter, def. 1.4), and a frozen reference policy and a frozen reward model (2 bytes per parameter in bf16).

For $N = 7 \times 10^9$, the states alone take
$$
2 \times 16N + 2 \times 2N = 36N \approx 252\ \text{GB},
$$
at least four 80 GB GPUs before any activation: ZeRO-3 (ch. 4) is not optional.

Per generated token, the rollout costs $2N$ FLOPs (policy), the scoring $2 \times 2N$ (reference and reward) and one PPO epoch $2 \times 6N$ (policy and value): about $18N$, three times the $6N$ of pre-training. The rollout is token-by-token decoding, hence memory-bound (def. 5.1): on the clock, generation typically dominates although it is a minority of the FLOPs. DPO ([LLMs ch. 5](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch5)) removes the value and reward models.
:::

### 7.3. Generative models {#dl-generative}

A generative model learns a distribution $p_\theta$ close to the data distribution $p_\mathrm{data}$, in order to sample new images, sounds or molecules. Autoregressive models were met in ch. 1 (text generation); the three other families below differ by how they make training tractable.

::: def
[Definition 7.7 — Variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling 2014)]{.tag} A latent variable $z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and a decoder $p_\theta(x \mid z)$ define $p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)p(z)\,dz$, an intractable integral.

An encoder
$$
q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma_\phi^2(x)\big)
$$
approximates the posterior, and training maximizes the evidence lower bound $$\mathrm{ELBO}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big),$$ a reconstruction term minus a regularization towards the prior.

Gradients with respect to $\phi$ go through the sampling by the **reparameterization** $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.8 — The ELBO is a lower bound, with an explicit gap (proved)]{.tag}

::: key
[Key result — the ELBO gap]{.tag}
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \mathrm{ELBO}(x) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) \geq \mathrm{ELBO}(x).
$$
:::

::: proof
By Bayes, $p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x \mid z)p(z)/p_\theta(x)$, so for every $z$:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log p(z) - \log p_\theta(z \mid x).
$$

Add and subtract $\log q_\phi(z \mid x)$ and take the expectation over $z \sim q_\phi(\cdot \mid x)$:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log\frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{p(z)}\big] + \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log\frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)}\big].
$$

The first two terms form the ELBO, the third is a KL divergence, which is non-negative. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.9 — The optimal GAN discriminator (Goodfellow et al. 2014, proved)]{.tag} A GAN trains a generator $G$ (pushing noise $z$ to samples of density $p_g$) against a discriminator $D(x) \in (0, 1)$ in the game
$$
\min_G\max_D\ \mathbb{E}_{p_\mathrm{data}}\log D(x) + \mathbb{E}_{p_g}\log(1 - D(x)).
$$

For a fixed generator, the best discriminator is
$$
D^\star(x) = \frac{p_\mathrm{data}(x)}{p_\mathrm{data}(x) + p_g(x)},
$$
and the value of the game becomes $2\,\mathrm{JS}(p_\mathrm{data}\,\|\,p_g) - \log 4$: the generator minimizes the Jensen–Shannon divergence, which is zero exactly when $p_g = p_\mathrm{data}$.

::: proof
The objective is
$$
\int\big(p_\mathrm{data}(x)\log D(x) + p_g(x)\log(1 - D(x))\big)dx,
$$
maximized pointwise.

For $a, b > 0$, $y \mapsto a\log y + b\log(1 - y)$ is concave on $(0, 1)$ with derivative $a/y - b/(1 - y)$, which vanishes at $y = a/(a + b)$: this gives $D^\star$.

With $m = (p_\mathrm{data} + p_g)/2$, the value is
$$
\mathbb{E}_{p_\mathrm{data}}\log\frac{p_\mathrm{data}}{2m} + \mathbb{E}_{p_g}\log\frac{p_g}{2m} = \mathrm{KL}(p_\mathrm{data}\|m) + \mathrm{KL}(p_g\|m) - 2\log 2 = 2\,\mathrm{JS}(p_\mathrm{data}\|p_g) - \log 4.
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 7.10 — Denoising diffusion (Ho, Jain & Abbeel 2020)]{.tag} A fixed forward process adds Gaussian noise in $T$ small steps,
$$
x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t ;
$$
it has the closed form
$$
x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon
$$
with $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \leq t}(1 - \beta_s)$ and $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.

A network $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ is trained to recover the noise, by minimizing
$$
\mathbb{E}_{x_0, t, \varepsilon}\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t\big)\big\|^2
$$
— a plain regression.

Sampling starts from pure noise $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and removes the predicted noise step by step.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.11 — How fast the forward process destroys an image, and what sampling costs]{.tag} With a constant $\beta_t = 0.02$, after $100$ steps
$$
\bar\alpha = 0.98^{100} \approx 0.133 :
$$
the image survives with coefficient $\sqrt{0.133} \approx 0.36$ under noise of standard deviation $\sqrt{0.867} \approx 0.93$.

With the schedule of Ho et al. ($T = 1\,000$, $\beta_t$ increasing linearly from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$), $\sum_t\beta_t \approx 10$ and
$$
\bar\alpha_T \approx e^{-10} \approx 4 \times 10^{-5} :
$$
$x_T$ is pure noise to excellent accuracy, which justifies starting the sampler there.

The cost side, in the language of this module: a GAN generates a sample in one forward pass, a diffusion model in up to $1\,000$ passes of its network (tens with modern samplers), and an autoregressive model in one pass per token — numbers that decide the inference budgets of ch. 5.
:::

  Family              Training signal                   Exact likelihood       Sampling cost                   Typical weakness
  ------------------- --------------------------------- ---------------------- ------------------------------- ---------------------------------
  autoregressive      next-token cross-entropy          yes                    one pass per token              slow sequential sampling
  VAE                 ELBO                              lower bound            one pass                        blurry samples
  GAN                 adversarial game                  no                     one pass                        unstable training, mode collapse
  diffusion           noise regression                  bound (variational)    tens to $1\,000$ passes         slow sampling

Diffusion, latent diffusion and text-to-image models are developed in [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html), optional reading since it is in the same choose-1 group as this course; [section 9.4 of the P1 Deep Learning notes](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#diffusion) gives the one-page version with guidance and code.

## 8. Theoretical complexity of training {#ch8}

The previous chapters made each training step faster with more GPUs; this chapter asks whether there is a *limit* to what parallelism can buy. The answer is yes, and it is *provable*: for distributed optimization over a network, lower bounds say how many computation and communication rounds any algorithm needs. This chapter is the most theoretical of the module, and its lower bound is the central result of the papers read in ch. 9.

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Decentralized distributed optimization over a graph]{.tag} $P$ machines, each with its own convex function $f_i$, connected by a graph $G$ (each machine talks only to its neighbors); common goal: $$\min_x\; f(x) = \frac{1}{P}\sum_{i=1}^{P} f_i(x).$$ The **execution time** counts two currencies: the number of *local* iterations (compute: a number of gradients that grows with the condition number $\kappa = L/\mu$ of [Machine Learning definition 0.4](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#gd-sgd)) and the **communication rounds** (one gossip round = mixing the vectors between neighbors).

The gossip matrix $W$ is symmetric and doubly stochastic, with $W_{ij} > 0$ only between neighbours.

The quality of the network is summarized by $\gamma \in [0,1)$, the second largest eigenvalue of $W$ in modulus, or equivalently by the **spectral gap** $1 - \gamma$.

The disagreement between machines shrinks like $\gamma^t$ after $t$ gossip rounds — the closer $\gamma$ is to $1$, the slower the network reaches consensus.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — The spectral gap of a ring and of a complete graph]{.tag} On a ring of $P$ machines where each one averages its value with its two neighbours, $W = \tfrac13(I + S + S^{-1})$ with $S$ the cyclic shift.

The eigenvalues of $W$ are $\tfrac13\big(1 + 2\cos(2\pi k/P)\big)$, $k = 0, \dots, P-1$; the largest is $1$ (consensus) and the second largest gives
$$
1 - \gamma = \tfrac43\sin^2(\pi/P) \approx \frac{4\pi^2}{3P^2}.
$$

For $P = 64$, $1 - \gamma \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-3}$ and $1/\sqrt{1-\gamma} \approx 18$: information needs a number of rounds proportional to $P$ to cross the ring.

On a complete graph with $W = \tfrac1P \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$, one round averages everything: $\gamma = 0$ and $1/\sqrt{1-\gamma} = 1$. The topology alone changes the communication factor by more than an order of magnitude.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.3 — Lower bounds and optimality (Scaman, Bach, Bubeck, Lee, Massoulié, ICML 2017; statement)]{.tag} For $f = \frac1P \sum f_i$ $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth ($\kappa = L/\mu$), *every* distributed algorithm (in the sense of def. 8.1) requires, to reach precision $\varepsilon$, a time

::: key
[Key result — the compute × communication lower bound]{.tag}
$$
T \;=\; \Omega\!\Big(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\Big(1 + \frac{\tau}{\sqrt{1-\gamma}}\Big)\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\Big),
$$
:::

where a local gradient computation takes one unit of time and a communication round takes $\tau$ units.

This order is **attained**, up to replacing the global condition number by the local ones of the $f_i$, by accelerated gradient ascent on the dual problem (Nesterov's accelerated scheme, which needs $O(\sqrt\kappa\,\ln(1/\varepsilon))$ gradient steps where gradient descent needs $O(\kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon))$; ch. 3 of the Optimization for AI notes is optional reading) combined with *Chebyshev accelerated gossip* — replacing $W$ by a well-chosen polynomial in $W$ that flattens its spectrum, the same trick that accelerates gradients, applied to the graph (the MSDA algorithm).

When communication dominates ($\tau$ large), the time is essentially $\tau\sqrt{\kappa/(1-\gamma)}\,\ln(1/\varepsilon)$: the product of the two obstacles. The JMLR 2019 version extends the analysis to non-smooth convex objectives.

::: proof
*Sketch of the lower bound (the "adversary" argument).* One constructs a family of "local" quadratics at each node, whose solution $x^\star$ depends on spread-out information.

For machine $i$ to learn what machine $j$ knew, the information must travel along the graph, and the *mixing of the graph* imposes $\Omega(1/\sqrt{1-\gamma})$ communication rounds (each gossip multiplies the imbalance by only $\gamma$).

Independently, even sequentially, a quadratic with condition number $\kappa$ requires $\Omega(\sqrt\kappa)$ gradient accesses (Nesterov's lower bound, Nesterov 2004, section 2.1).

The construction crosses the two obstacles into a quadratic *on the product* graph × condition number: no algorithm can beat the product of the two bounds. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Reading: the two regimes, and why they structure practice]{.tag}

| Regime | Condition | Dominant time | Practical equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| **sequential (compute)** | fast network, small $\gamma$ (NVLink, $\gamma \approx 0.1$) | $\sqrt{\kappa}$: Nesterov reigns | a single node, 8 tightly linked GPUs |
| **parallel (communication)** | slow network, $\gamma \to 1$ (Ethernet, large clusters) | $\sqrt{\kappa/(1-\gamma)}$: the network caps everything | multi-datacenter, federated (see the Emerging ML module, ch. 2–3) |

Engineering consequence: **adding machines does not reduce the time below the communication floor**. This is the exact analogue of Amdahl's law (ch. 6) for optimization: the "sequential" part is no longer a program but the geometry of the network. All of ch. 3 (all-reduce, compression, overlap) is a war against this $\sqrt{1/(1-\gamma)}$.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.4 — What parallelism *can* buy: the "finite sum" regime]{.tag} The bound of theorem 8.3 concerns the time to *reach* an $\varepsilon$-optimal point when the data are *partitioned* (each $f_i$ is opaque). If instead all machines can evaluate the *same* function (replicated data), parallelism reduces the variance of SGD (mini-batching divides the gradient variance by the batch size) — but the optimal statistical rate bounds the gain (Dieuleveut et al.; ch. 5 and 11 of the Optimization for AI notes are optional reading). In short: parallelism speeds up *compute*, never (or marginally) the *statistical complexity* — a distinction that commercial announcements like to forget.
:::

## 9. Research readings: lower bounds and Lipschitz regularity {#ch9}

**Who wrote these papers (2026-2027 catalog):** the APM_52183_EP course unit “Apprentissage profond de la théorie à la pratique” is led by Boris Bonev (“Responsable” on the 2026–2027 sheet and on the track page), with P. Bianchi, C. Bonet and B. Bonev on the instructional engineering team.

The works presented below are those of Kevin Scaman (previously MSR–INRIA) and co-authors, the lower-bound results underlying chapter 8 and the Lipschitz analysis behind section 7.1. The curriculum wiki names Kevin Scaman as the instructor of this course, while the 2026–2027 sheet names Boris Bonev as responsible; either way, the papers are classic references of the field.

Three papers to know:

::: note
[Optimality of distributed optimization (the heart of ch. 8)]{.tag}

-   K. Scaman, F. Bach, S. Bubeck, Y. T. Lee, L. Massoulié, [Optimal Algorithms for Smooth and Strongly Convex Distributed Optimization in Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08704), ICML 2017 — the paper establishing the lower bound of theorem 8.3 *and* the optimal algorithm (Nesterov × Chebyshev gossip): the optimal time depends on the product condition number × topology. This is the first complete characterization of the compute/communication trade-off over networks.
-   K. Scaman, F. Bach, S. Bubeck, L. Massoulié, [Optimal Convergence Rates for Convex Distributed Optimization in Networks](http://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume20/19-543/19-543.pdf), JMLR 2019 — the journal version, extended to the non-strongly convex case: the two regimes of chapter 8 are characterized there optimally.
:::

::: note
[Complexity of neural networks: Lipschitz regularity]{.tag}

-   A. Virmaux, K. Scaman, [Lipschitz regularity of deep neural networks: analysis and efficient estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10965), NeurIPS 2018 — proving that computing *exactly* the Lipschitz constant of a deep network is NP-hard, and designing the estimator (SeqLip, layer-wise power iteration) that became standard. The link with this module: the quantization bound of the mixed-precision note of ch. 4 involves precisely these $\mathrm{Lip}_m$ constants — and the paper says how far one can (not) compute them; on the robustness side, the Lipschitz constant is the certificate of adversarial guarantees (see the M2 Security and Robustness module, ch. 5).
:::

::: note
[Reading thread]{.tag} L1: read the ICML 2017 focusing on (i) the construction of the lower bound (theorem 8.3 above); L2: re-prove the pipeline bubble (2.3) on paper; L3: profile a mini distributed training run (exercise 8) and empirically verify the ring all-reduce formula 3.2. This is the theory → system → measurement chain that defines this module.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Counting.** Prove the "per token" formula $24d^2 + 4nd$ of a transformer block (prop. 1.2), then verify theorem 1.3 on a GPT-2 small ($N \approx 124$M, 12 blocks, $d = 768$): compute $C$ for $D = 3$B tokens and compare with a `torch.profiler` (or `flops-profiler`) profile within ±10%. *Expected solution*: $6ND \approx 2.2\times10^{21}$ FLOPs.
2.  **★ Pipeline bubble.** Re-prove theorem 2.3 (draw the 1F1B Gantt chart for $p=4$, $m=8$). Then: what minimal $m$ for an efficiency ≥ 90% with $p = 16$ stages? *Solution*: $m/(m+15) \geq 0.9 \Rightarrow m \geq 135$.
3.  **★ Inference memory wall.** **(a)** Recover the KV cache formula (def. 5.1) for a model with grouped-query attention (GQA: $g$ head groups instead of $h$) — what saving?

    **(b)** Compute the peak throughput of a 13B fp16 on an A100 (2 TB/s) and on a 1 TB/s GPU.

    **(c)** Show that, as far as the weights are concerned, int8 doubles this ceiling and int4 quadruples it, and explain why batching raises the aggregate throughput but not this per-sequence ceiling.

    *Solution*: (a) factor $g/h$; (b) ≈ 77 then 38 tok/s; (c) the weights go from $2N$ bytes to $N$ (int8) and $N/2$ (int4): the ceiling is multiplied by $2$ and $4$, up to the KV cache, which stays in bf16.
4.  **★ Roofline.** A kernel reads $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and computes $Xw$ ($2mn$ FLOPs, $(mn + n + m)\times4$ bytes).

    **(a)** Intensity $I(m)$ as $m \to \infty$ (at fixed $n=4096$)?

    **(b)** On an A100 (312 TFLOP/s, 2 TB/s), for which $m$ is the GEMV memory-bound?

    **(c)** Deduce why autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and what batching changes there (hint: $I$ grows with batch size — but not the wall per token).
5.  **★★ All-reduce.** Prove theorem 3.2 on the reduce-scatter (induction on the steps).

    Then plot $T_\mathrm{ring}$ and $T_\mathrm{tree}$ (prop. 3.3) for $S = 1$ GB, $\alpha = 2\,\mu s$, $b = 25$ GB/s, $P = 2 \dots 512$ on a log scale. Crossover? Which mode for a bf16 LLM-13B gradient?

    *Partial solution*: the ring wins as soon as $S/P \gg \alpha b$.
6.  **★★ Checkpointing.** A model with 30 blocks, activations 1.2 GB per block, 15 GB of memory available for activations.

    **(a)** Verify that storing all the activations does not fit.

    **(b)** Apply theorem 4.1: how many segments, what memory, what time overhead?

    **(c)** Show that with a single level of checkpoints and $k$ segments the memory is about $(k + L/k)\,a$, hence never below $2\sqrt{L}\,a$; explain how recursive checkpointing goes below this floor at the price of more recomputation (Chen et al. 2016 reach $O(\log L)$ memory for $O(L \log L)$ computation).

    *Solution*: (a) $36$ GB $> 15$ GB; (b) $5$ or $6$ segments, $(5 + 6) \times 1.2 \approx 13.2$ GB, about $+\tfrac13$ of time.
7.  **★★ Complete budget (the capstone lab).** Take up the table 6.4 with $N = 13$B, $D = 300$B tokens (a "Chinchilla-lite" budget: comment on the $D/N$ ratio), on 64 H100 GPUs (≈ 990 TFLOP/s bf16, 40% MFU, 700 W). Compute: FLOPs, GPU-hours, calendar time, states memory (ZeRO-3 over 8 nodes?), energy, FR/world emissions. Conclude with three sentences of architecture recommendation.

    *Partial answers*: $2.3\times10^{22}$ FLOPs; ≈ 16,500 GPU·h; ≈ 11 days; 208 GB of states → ZeRO mandatory.
8.  **★★★ Paper + measurement.** Choose: Megatron (TP), ZeRO, or FlashAttention.

    **(a)** Summarize the mechanism in 10 lines with the module's formulas.

    **(b)** Measure an effect on a small real setup (2 GPUs suffice): DP scaling 1→2→4 on a model that fits in memory (verify the $\frac{2(P-1)}{P}\frac{S}{b}$ term of theorem 3.2 with `torch.distributed` and a barrier-timer).

    **(c)** Present in 10 minutes: key figure, one reproduced number, one limitation.

    *Grid*: accuracy of the quoted formulas, honesty of the measurement (error bars!), relevance of the chosen limitation.

### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

The sheet asks for validation by project, so the project carries most of the grade, with three milestone notebooks from the official themes 7–9. The counting questions below are asked at the defence (one per student, with new numbers) and can also serve as an optional, ungraded quiz.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project | 70 % | a card below, or Ex. 7 or 8 extended; report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) and 10-minute defence with one counting question | ch. 0–8 |
| Milestone notebooks | 30 % | three notebooks, 10 % each, due one week after the session | session 9 (FGSM on the CIFAR-10 model of session 1), session 10 (REINFORCE on a small control task), session 11 (a small VAE or DDPM on MNIST) |
| Counting quiz (optional) | 0 % | 1 h, calculator allowed, after session 8; formative | ch. 1–6 |

**Resit.** An individual oral on the project (an improved report is allowed) with one counting question; as on the sheet, the final grade is the maximum of the two grades.

**Sample questions.** Five counting questions worth 20 points make the 1 h quiz, calculator allowed: three computations, one derivation, and one diagnosis.

**Q1 (4 pts) — Training compute and memory.** A dense transformer of $N = 1.3 \times 10^9$ parameters is trained with the Chinchilla ratio $D = 20N$, with Adam in mixed precision, on 8 A100 GPUs (312 TFLOP/s in bf16) at 40 % MFU. (a) Give the number of tokens and the total FLOPs. (b) Give the training time. (c) Give the memory of the training states, and say whether plain data parallelism fits on 80 GB GPUs.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $D = 2.6 \times 10^{10}$ tokens; theorem 1.3 gives $C = 6ND \approx 2.03 \times 10^{20}$ FLOPs (1.5 pts).
- (b) The cluster delivers $8 \times 312 \times 0.4 \approx 1\,000$ TFLOP/s, so the run takes about $2.0 \times 10^5$ s, that is 56 h or 2.4 days (1 pt).
- (c) Definition 1.4: 16 bytes per parameter, so 20.8 GB of states, replicated on each GPU by plain data parallelism; this fits in 80 GB with room for activations, and checkpointing (theorem 4.1) is the fallback if they grow (1.5 pts). Common error: 2 bytes per parameter (the weights alone), or forgetting the $4ND$ of the backward pass.
:::

**Q2 (4 pts) — KV cache and the decoding wall.** A 13B model with 40 layers and $d = 5120$ is served in bf16 on one 80 GB GPU with 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. (a) Give the KV cache of one sequence of 4,096 tokens. (b) How many such sequences fit next to the weights? (c) Give the ceiling on tokens per second for one sequence, and say what batching changes.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Definition 5.1: $4 \times 40 \times 4096 \times 5120 \approx 3.36 \times 10^9$ bytes, about 3.4 GB (1.5 pts).
- (b) The weights take $2N = 26$ GB, so $(80 - 26)/3.36 \approx 16$ sequences, before activations and fragmentation (1 pt).
- (c) Every token rereads all the weights: $2 \times 10^{12} / 2.6 \times 10^{10} \approx 77$ tokens/s per sequence. Batching serves $B$ sequences per read and raises the aggregate throughput until memory (here about 16 sequences) or compute (around $B \approx 150$, example 6.2) runs out, but not the per-sequence ceiling (1.5 pts). Common error: forgetting the factor 2 for K and V, or the 2 bytes of bf16.
:::

**Q3 (4 pts) — Pipeline bubble and all-reduce.** (a) A pipeline of $p = 8$ stages processes $m = 24$ micro-batches under 1F1B: give the efficiency and the bubble fraction, and the smallest $m$ for 90 % efficiency. (b) A gradient of $S = 2$ GB is all-reduced over $P = 16$ machines with latency 5 µs and bandwidth 50 GB/s: give the ring and tree times, say which wins, and why.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Theorem 2.3: efficiency $24/31 \approx 0.77$, bubble $7/31 \approx 23\,\%$; $m/(m + 7) \geq 0.9$ gives $m \geq 63$ (2 pts).
- (b) With $S/b = 40$ ms, theorem 3.2 and proposition 3.3 give
    $$
    T_\mathrm{ring} = 2 \times 15 \times 5\ \mu\text{s} + \tfrac{30}{16} \times 40\ \text{ms} \approx 75\ \text{ms}, \qquad T_\mathrm{tree} = 2 \times 4 \times (5\ \mu\text{s} + 40\ \text{ms}) \approx 320\ \text{ms}.
    $$
    The ring wins by a factor of about 4: for a large message bandwidth dominates, and the ring sends less than $2S$ per machine where the tree sends $S$ at each of its $2\log_2 P$ steps (2 pts). Common error: $\log_2 P$ steps instead of $2\log_2 P$ for the tree.
:::

**Q4 (4 pts) — The 6ND rule.** (a) Show that a linear layer applied to $n$ tokens costs 2 FLOPs per parameter and per token. (b) Explain why the backward pass costs twice the forward pass, and deduce theorem 1.3. (c) For GPT-2 small ($d = 768$, $n = 1024$), compare the two terms of the per-token cost $24d^2 + 4nd$ of a block, and say when the rule stops being accurate.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Each output coordinate of $Wx$ is a dot product of length $d_\mathrm{in}$: $d_\mathrm{in}d_\mathrm{out}$ multiply-adds, that is $2d_\mathrm{in}d_\mathrm{out}$ FLOPs per token for $d_\mathrm{in}d_\mathrm{out}$ parameters (1 pt).
- (b) The backward pass forms the input gradient $W^\top\delta$ and the weight gradient $\delta x^\top$, each 2 FLOPs per parameter and per token: $4ND$, so $2ND + 4ND = 6ND$ (1.5 pts).
- (c) $24d^2 \approx 14.2$ M and $4nd \approx 3.1$ M FLOPs per token: the matrix products dominate. The terms are equal at $n = 6d \approx 4\,600$ tokens; beyond, the quadratic attention term takes over and $6ND$ underestimates the cost (1.5 pts). Common error: counting a multiply-add as one FLOP.
:::

**Q5 (4 pts) — A disappointing speedup.** A training script runs only 1.2 times faster on 8 GPUs than on 1. (a) Under Amdahl's law, what fraction $s$ of the single-GPU step time is not parallelized? (b) What is the best speedup on 64 GPUs with the same $s$? (c) Name two likely causes that a profile would show, and the measurement that tells them apart.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Proposition 6.3: $1/1.2 = s + (1 - s)/8$, so $s = (1/1.2 - 1/8)/(7/8) \approx 0.81$ (1.5 pts).
- (b) $1/(0.81 + 0.19/64) \approx 1.23$, against the ceiling $1/s \approx 1.24$: more GPUs are useless until the serial part shrinks (1 pt).
- (c) Two of: data loading on the CPU (too few loader workers: the GPUs wait for input), a gradient all-reduce not overlapped with compute (ch. 3: buckets and overlap), host–device synchronizations such as `.item()` at every step. The profiler timeline separates input wait, communication and compute (1.5 pts). Common error: blaming the FLOP/s of the GPU, which the roofline of ch. 6 rules out here.
:::

In Year 2, the serving datasheets of capstones [C1](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c1), [C4](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c4) and [C8](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c8) (P50/P99 latency, cost and energy per 1,000 requests) apply the four-column protocol of example 5.4 at scale; card P3 rehearses it.
